Cell Division & the Cell Cycle

Why cells divide, and the three kinds of division side by side: binary fission, mitosis and meiosis, and who does each. Then this module goes in depth on the two that copy DNA, binary fission and mitosis, with the cell cycle, haploid and diploid, and the human karyotype. Meiosis, the division that mixes DNA, gets its own deep dive in Module 3.2.

MODULE 3.1 · PART 1

Why and how cells divide

THE QUESTION Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. How does one cell become two, each with a complete copy of the DNA, and which cells divide which way?

In this part: why cells divide, the two jobs of every division (replication and segregation), the three kinds of division side by side, copying vs. mixing DNA, asexual vs. sexual reproduction, where the DNA is in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and binary fission step by step.

START HERE

Why do cells divide?

Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Cell division is how one cell becomes two, and there are several reasons a living thing needs it.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR SCENES

One process, four jobs

Tap a button to explore
1 · ONE-CELLED ORGANISMSDivision is reproductionFor a unicellular organism, such as a bacterium or a yeast, dividing in two is making offspring. Each daughter cell is a new organism.
2 · DEVELOPMENT AND GROWTHFrom one cell to a whole bodyYou started as a single cell, a fertilized egg. Mitosis turned it into the trillions of cells you are made of, and growth still depends on it.
3 · REPAIR AND REGENERATIONReplacing what is lostScrape your knee and the cells around the wound divide to fill the gap. Your body also keeps replacing worn-out skin cells, blood cells and the cells lining your gut.
4 · ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONA new organism from one parentSome multicellular species reproduce asexually by mitosis. A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a new plant with the same DNA.
TAP A SCENEAt least three reasonsCells divide for reproduction, for development and growth, and for repair and regeneration. Tap each scene.
REPRODUCTIONMake a new organismOne-celled organisms, and some multicellular species that reproduce asexually.
GROWTHBuild a bodyDevelopment from one fertilized egg into an adult.
REPAIRFix and replaceHealing wounds and replacing worn-out cells.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Unicellular

Made of a single cell. For a unicellular organism, cell division is reproduction.

COPY, THEN SHARE

Replication, then segregation

Whatever the reason, and whatever kind of cell, every cell division has the same two parts. First the cell copies its DNA. Then it hands one copy to each daughter cell.

INTERACTIVE · ONE CELL BECOMES TWO

Copy, then share

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
STARTOne cell, one set of DNAThe parent cell has its DNA. To make two complete cells, it needs two complete copies.
PART 1 · REPLICATIONCopy the DNAThe cell replicates its DNA: it makes an exact copy of every DNA molecule. The two copies stay joined for now.
PART 2 · SEGREGATIONSend one copy to each daughter cellThe copies are segregated, pulled apart into two daughter cells. Each daughter gets one full copy.
THREE KINDS OF DIVISION, SAME TWO JOBSBinary fission, mitosis and meiosis all replicate the DNA and then segregate the copies. What differs is who does each one, where the DNA is, and what comes out. They are side by side a little further down.
COMMON MIX-UPReplication and segregation are not the same thing. Replication makes the copies. Segregation separates the copies into different cells. A cell that replicated but did not segregate would just have twice the DNA.
WHO'S WHO, AND WHERE THE DNA IS

Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes

Every living thing belongs to one of three domains. Two of them, bacteria and archaea, are prokaryotes; the third is the eukaryotes. Which group an organism is in tells you where its DNA is and how its cells divide.

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE OF LIFE

Three domains, and what each one does

Tap a button to explore
BACTERIA · PROKARYOTESOne cell, no nucleusBacteria such as E. coli are always unicellular. Their DNA is one circular chromosome, often with plasmids, with no nucleus around it.They reproduce by binary fission, which is asexual, and can pass DNA to each other by conjugation.
ARCHAEA · PROKARYOTESLook like bacteria, related to usArchaea (for example the microbes that make methane in swamps and cow stomachs) are also unicellular prokaryotes with circular DNA, and also divide by binary fission.On the tree, though, archaea are the closest relatives of eukaryotes. For cell division, treat bacteria and archaea as one group: prokaryotes.
EUKARYA · EUKARYOTESA nucleus, and one cell or manyEukaryotes keep their linear chromosomes in a nucleus. Some are unicellular (yeast, amoebas); others are multicellular (animals, plants, most fungi).Their cells divide by mitosis, and the germ cells of sexually reproducing species also divide by meiosis.
ALL THREEThe mind mapProkaryotes (bacteria, archaea): one cell, no nucleus, binary fission. Eukaryotes: a nucleus, mitosis and meiosis. The rest of this section zooms in on where the DNA sits.
TAP A DOMAINThe tree of lifeThree branches from one common ancestor. Tap a domain to see what it does.
UNICELLULAR · ONE CELLMULTICELLULAR · MANY CELLS
WhoAll bacteria and archaea; some eukaryotes: yeast, amoebas, Paramecium, many algaeOnly eukaryotes: animals, plants, most fungi (mushrooms, molds), seaweeds such as kelp
One cell divisionMakes a new organism: division is reproductionMakes more cells in the same body, for growth and repair
ReproductionBinary fission (prokaryotes) or mitosis (yeast, amoebas)Asexual, by mitosis (runners, budding), or sexual, by meiosis and fertilization
INTERACTIVE · WHERE, WHAT SHAPE, AND HOW IT FITS

Where is the DNA?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
WHERE · PROKARYOTESOne place: loose in the cellA bacterium or archaeon has no nucleus. Its DNA sits in the cytoplasm, held on the cell membrane. Almost all its genes are on one circular chromosome.Plasmids are small extra circles of DNA, usually with genes that are not essential, such as one for resisting an antibiotic.
WHERE · EUKARYOTESThree places, two shapesThe nucleus holds most of the DNA, as linear chromosomes: this is the nuclear DNA, what "genome" usually means.Mitochondria, and the chloroplasts of plants and algae, each hold their own small circle of DNA. They came from bacteria long ago (Module 2.2), which is why their DNA is circular and they still divide by binary fission.
HOW IT FITS · ZOOM INNucleus, chromosome, DNA, gene: one inside the otherThese are not four separate places. They are zoom levels of the same thing.The nucleus holds the chromosomes. Each chromosome is one long double-stranded DNA molecule, wound on proteins. A gene is one stretch of that DNA, and one chromosome carries many genes.
OVER TIME · THE CELL CYCLESame DNA, different packingStages change how the DNA is packed, not where it is. Between divisions (interphase) the chromosomes are long, loose threads, so genes can be read and the DNA copied.Before the cell divides they condense into compact X shapes that are easy to move. Part 2 follows this step by step.
PROKARYOTES (BACTERIA, ARCHAEA)EUKARYOTES
NucleusNone, and no other compartmentsYes, plus other compartments
ChromosomesOne, circularUsually several, linear
Extra DNAPlasmids: small, usually non-essential genesCircular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts
DNA attached toThe cell membraneNot the membrane: inside the nucleus
How they divideBinary fissionMitosis (body cells) and meiosis (germ cells)
Check yourself: Why do mitochondria and chloroplasts contain circular DNA?

Because they were once free-living bacteria. An ancestral cell engulfed them (endosymbiosis), and they kept the circular DNA bacteria have. They still divide by binary fission.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Multicellular

Made of many cells, like animals, plants and most fungi. Only eukaryotes are multicellular. Cell division builds and repairs the body; reproduction is a separate job.

Plasmid

A small circle of DNA in a prokaryotic cell, separate from the chromosome. It usually carries genes that are not essential for the species.

Chromosome

One double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins. It carries many genes. After S phase it is two sister chromatids, but it still counts as one chromosome.

Nuclear DNA

The DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, organized into linear chromosomes. In eukaryotes, "genome" usually means the nuclear DNA.

WHO DOES WHICH?

Binary fission, mitosis and meiosis

There are three kinds of cell division. Which one a cell uses depends on whether it is a prokaryote or a eukaryote, and, in eukaryotes, on whether it is a body cell or a germ cell.

THREE KINDS OF ORGANISM

Who divides how?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEABinary fission, and that's itA bacterium or an archaeon is unicellular: one cell is the whole organism. To reproduce, it copies its DNA and splits in two by binary fission. That is asexual reproduction: one parent, two identical offspring.Prokaryotes have no nucleus and never do mitosis or meiosis.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE SEXUALLYMitosis and meiosis in the same bodyIn an animal or a flowering plant, the somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis: 2 identical cells, for growth and repair. Only the germ cells (in ovaries and testes, or in flowers) divide by meiosis: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes, all different.Here mitosis is not reproduction. Reproduction is meiosis (to make gametes) plus fertilization, a gamete from each of two parents.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE ASEXUALLYMitosis only, no meiosisMany eukaryotes also make offspring by mitosis alone: yeast grows buds, a strawberry plant sends out runners, and female aphids have young without mating. One parent, no mate, and the offspring are clones.Many species do both, depending on conditions (strawberries also flower). So prokaryotes are always asexual, but eukaryotes can be asexual, sexual or both.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis vs. meiosis is not just about where it happens. Yes, mitosis is in body cells and meiosis only in germ cells. But they are different processes with different results: mitosis gives 2 identical cells (2n → 2n); meiosis gives 4 different gametes with half the chromosomes (2n → n).
COMMON MIX-UPProkaryotes = asexual, but eukaryotes ≠ always sexual. Binary fission is always asexual. Eukaryotes can reproduce asexually by mitosis (yeast, strawberries), sexually by meiosis and fertilization (people), or both.
INTERACTIVE · SIDE BY SIDE

Three kinds of division

Tap a button to explore
BINARY FISSION · PROKARYOTESBacteria and archaeaWho: prokaryotes, which are bacteria and archaea (for cell division they work the same way). Also mitochondria and chloroplasts inside eukaryotic cells.The DNA: one circular chromosome (plus plasmids), no nucleus, attached to the cell membrane.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent. For a one-celled prokaryote, that is reproduction.
MITOSIS · EUKARYOTESSomatic (body) cellsWho: eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists), in their somatic (body) cells. In a eukaryote that reproduces asexually, mitosis is also how it makes offspring.The DNA: several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent (2n → 2n), for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
MEIOSIS · EUKARYOTESGerm cells onlyWho: eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, and only in germ cells, the cells that make eggs and sperm. The same organism does mitosis in all its other cells: that is why the dashed box joins the two.Two divisions in a row: meiosis I splits each homologous pair (A from a) into 2 cells; meiosis II splits the sister chromatids, like mitosis, into 4 gametes. No DNA copying in between.The DNA: linear chromosomes in a nucleus, in homologous pairs (A from the mother, a from the father).Result: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes (2n → n) and different DNA, for sexual reproduction. How it works is Module 3.2.
ALL THREETwo categories, same two jobsBinary fission is its own category (prokaryotes). Mitosis and meiosis belong together (eukaryotes). Each one replicates the DNA and then segregates the copies. Binary fission segregates by the cell growing; mitosis and meiosis need a spindle to pull chromosomes apart.
TAP ONEWhich cells do which?Prokaryotes do only binary fission. Eukaryotes do mitosis and meiosis, never binary fission (except inside their mitochondria and chloroplasts).
BINARY FISSIONProkaryotesBacteria and archaea · circular chromosome, no nucleus · 2 identical cells · reproduction
MITOSISEukaryote body cellsLinear chromosomes in a nucleus · 2 identical cells · 2n → 2n · growth, repair, asexual reproduction
MEIOSISEukaryote germ cells onlyLinear chromosomes in a nucleus · 4 different gametes · 2n → n · sexual reproduction
COMMON MIX-UPMeiosis I and meiosis II are not generations. They are two divisions in a row inside one meiosis: 1 germ cell → 2 cells (meiosis I, homologous pairs separate) → 4 gametes (meiosis II, sister chromatids separate). The next generation only starts at fertilization. Module 3.2 goes through both step by step.
COMMON MIX-UPBacteria never do mitosis or meiosis. Prokaryotes divide only by binary fission. Mitosis and meiosis happen only in eukaryotes: mitosis gives 2 identical cells, meiosis gives 4 gametes with different DNA.
Check yourself: What results from mitosis, and how could a mutation change that?

Two daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent. A mutation, a change that happens by chance when the DNA is copied, makes the copies differ slightly, so a daughter cell can carry a new mutation the parent cell did not have.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Mitosis

Division of the nucleus in which the sister chromatids of every chromosome are pulled apart, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent cell.

Meiosis

The cell division that turns a diploid cell into four haploid gametes, whose DNA is different from the parent cell's.

ONE PARENT OR TWO?

Asexual vs. sexual reproduction

"Asexual" and "sexual" describe how a whole organism makes offspring, not a kind of cell. A strawberry plant sending out runners is reproducing asexually, by mitosis. Two people having a child are reproducing sexually, by meiosis and fertilization.

ONE PARENT OR TWO · WHAT COMES OUT

Clones vs. a family

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONOne parent, identical offspringOne plant makes new plants by mitosis only, for example along runners. No second organism is needed. The offspring are clones: the same genotype as the parent, so they look the same too.The only way a clone differs is a new mutation, a chance change when the DNA is copied.
SEXUAL REPRODUCTIONTwo parents, a new mix every timeA female (♀) and a male (♂) each make gametes by meiosis, which deals each gamete one allele of every gene, at random. Fertilization joins an egg and a sperm.Here the mother is Hh Cc and the father hh cc, so four different kids are possible. Every child is a recombination of the parents' genes, not a copy of either one. (The hair genes are made up for the picture.)
GENOTYPE VS. PHENOTYPEThe letters vs. the lookEvery organism, plant, animal or microbe, has both. Genotype = the alleles it carries (PP, Pp, pp). Phenotype = what you can see or measure (purple flowers, height, spiky hair).Different genotypes can give the same phenotype: PP and Pp flowers are both purple, because P hides p (dominant and recessive alleles are Module 3.3). And the same genotype can give different phenotypes: two Pp clones grow tall in sun and short in shade.
ASEXUALSEXUAL
WhoProkaryotes always; many eukaryotes (yeast, strawberry runners, aphids)Most animals and plants, many fungi
ParentsOne, no mate neededTwo: a female and a male gamete
DivisionBinary fission or mitosis, no meiosisMeiosis, then fertilization
OffspringClones: same genotype as the parentNew mixes: every genotype different
GO DEEPERGenotypes, phenotypes and predicting the kids of a cross are in Module 3.3.
WHY TWO WAYS?

Fast copies vs. a shuffled deck

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
THE PRICE OF SEXAsexual populations grow fasterSay every female has 2 offspring. 100 asexual females make 200 offspring, all able to reproduce: the population doubles. 100 sexual individuals are about half males, so they make 100 offspring: the population only replaces itself.The cost comes from needing males (only females produce offspring), not from meiosis being a slower division.
THE SHUFFLEEvery gamete is a different handMeiosis deals each gamete one chromosome from every pair, at random. With 3 pairs there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 possible hands; with your 23 pairs, 2²³, about 8 million. Then fertilization combines two hands.
THE PAYOFFA moving targetParasites and viruses adapt to the host genotypes that are common. If every host is a copy, one virus that fits one fits all. If every host is a new shuffle, it fits only a few, and the next generation is shuffled again. That is why sex allows rapid adaptation to new environments and parasites.
ASEXUALSEXUAL
AdvantagesSaves energy, no mates, faster growthHigh genetic variability, rapid adaptation
DisadvantagesLow variability, slow to adaptCosts energy, only females have young
GO DEEPERThe full trade-offs and how many gametes the shuffle can make are in Module 3.2.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Asexual reproduction

Reproduction by one parent alone, by mitosis (or binary fission in prokaryotes). The offspring have the same DNA as the parent, except new mutations.

Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilization, so the offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Genotype

The alleles an organism carries for a gene or genes, written as letters such as Hh. Clones have the same genotype.

Phenotype

What an organism looks like or does: its observable traits, such as hair shape. It depends on the genotype and on the environment.

COPY OR MIX?

Genetically identical copies vs. recombination

Every way of handling DNA either makes genetically identical copies (same DNA out) or causes recombination (new combinations of genes). Prokaryotes and eukaryotes each have a way to do both, but only eukaryotes recombine while making offspring.

INTERACTIVE · TWO JOBS × TWO KINDS OF CELL

Identical copies or recombination?

Tap a button to explore
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEACopy by dividing, recombine without dividingCopy: binary fission makes 2 cells with the same DNA. That is how prokaryotes reproduce.Recombine: separately, one cell can pass a copy of some DNA, often a plasmid, to another through a bridge: conjugation. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction, and it is not meiosis.
EUKARYOTESMitosis copies, meiosis recombinesCopy: mitosis makes 2 cells with the same DNA, in body cells and in asexual reproduction.Recombine: meiosis deals each gamete a different combination of the parents' chromosomes, and fertilization joins two of them: sexual reproduction.
GENETICALLY IDENTICAL COPIESBinary fission and mitosis are the same ideaBoth copy the DNA and split it evenly: 2 identical cells. Binary fission is the prokaryote version, mitosis the eukaryote version. They differ in how the copies are pulled apart (membrane growth vs. a spindle).
RECOMBINATIONConjugation and meiosis both recombine genes, very differentlyConjugation (prokaryotes): DNA passes from one cell to another; no division, no gametes.Meiosis + fertilization (eukaryotes): chromosomes are shuffled into gametes, then two gametes fuse.
TAP A ROW OR COLUMNTwo ways to handle DNAIdentical copies keep the DNA the same. Recombination makes new combinations of genes. And mutation adds brand-new changes in all four.
COMMON MIX-UPBinary fission is not a kind of meiosis. It is the prokaryote way of making identical copies, like mitosis. Bacteria recombine DNA by conjugation, which is not cell division at all.
Check yourself: Do bacteria shuffle their DNA the way humans do in meiosis?

No. Bacteria never do meiosis. They can share DNA by conjugation, passing a copy of a plasmid or other DNA to a neighbor, which also creates new combinations of genes. But it happens apart from reproduction: binary fission itself just copies.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Conjugation

A way prokaryotes share DNA: one cell passes a copy of some of its DNA, often a plasmid, to another cell through a connecting bridge. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction.

HOW PROKARYOTES DIVIDE

Binary fission, step by step

Bacteria and archaea divide by binary fission. It has the same two jobs, replication and segregation, and it is the simplest way to do them.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR STAGES

One bacterium becomes two

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
1 · BEFOREDNA attached to the membraneThe circular chromosome is held to the inside of the cell membrane by a protein.
2 · REPLICATIONCopying the circleReplication starts at one spot on the circle and runs both ways around it. The result is two circles, each attached to the membrane.
3 · SEGREGATION BY GROWTHThe cell lengthensAs the cell grows longer, the two attachment points move apart, carrying the two circles to opposite ends. Growth itself does the separating.
4 · DIVISIONTwo daughter cellsThe cell pinches in at the middle and new membrane and wall form. Each daughter cell has the same DNA as the parent cell.
WHAT SETS THE SPEED?Binary fission is regulated by nutrient availability. With plenty of nutrients, a bacterium copies its DNA and divides quickly. When nutrients run short, division slows down or stops.
NOT ONLY BACTERIAMitochondria and chloroplasts also divide by binary fission inside your cells, the way the bacteria they came from did (Module 2.2).
Check yourself: Why can a bacterium or archaeon separate its DNA just by growing, when a eukaryotic cell cannot?

Because a bacterium's DNA is attached to the cell membrane. As the cell grows, the membrane carries the two copies apart. A eukaryotic cell's DNA is inside a nucleus, not on the membrane, so it needs another way to pull the copies apart: mitosis.

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Cells divide to reproduce (one-celled organisms, asexual reproduction), to grow from one fertilized egg, and to repair and replace tissues.
  2. Every division has two jobs: replicate the DNA, then segregate the copies into two daughter cells.
  3. Three domains: bacteria and archaea (prokaryotes, always unicellular) and eukaryotes (unicellular like yeast, or multicellular like animals and plants).
  4. Binary fission: prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) → 2 identical cells. Mitosis: eukaryote body cells → 2 identical cells. Meiosis: eukaryote germ cells only → 4 different gametes. Bacteria never do mitosis or meiosis.
  5. Prokaryotes: no nucleus, one circular chromosome attached to the membrane, often plasmids. Binary fission is regulated by nutrient availability.
  6. Eukaryotes: usually several linear chromosomes in the nucleus (the genome). Mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA because they came from bacteria.
  7. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule carrying many genes.
  8. Asexual: one parent, mitosis (or binary fission) only, clones. Sexual: two parents, meiosis and fertilization, every child a new mix. Genotype = the alleles; phenotype = the look.
  9. Identical copies: binary fission, mitosis. Recombination: conjugation (prokaryotes, not reproduction), meiosis and fertilization (eukaryotes).
MODULE 3.1 · PART 2

The eukaryotic cell cycle

THE QUESTION Before a eukaryotic cell can divide, every chromosome has to be copied. When does that happen, and what does a chromosome look like before and after?

In this part: the complete cycle from G1 to cytokinesis, what a chromosome looks like through it, and how to count chromosomes and DNA molecules.

THE WHOLE CYCLE

The cell cycle, G1 to cytokinesis

A eukaryotic cell does not divide whenever it likes. Its life runs in a cycle, and checkpoints make sure it is ready before each stage. Follow one cell all the way round: it has 4 chromosomes, a long pair and a short pair, one of each pair from the mother (pink) and one from the father (blue).

INTERACTIVE · THE COMPLETE CYCLE

Eight stages, one cell, every chromosome

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 8
INTERPHASE · G1 (GAP 1)GrowThe cell grows and replicates its organelles. Each chromosome is unreplicated: one DNA molecule. 4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules.The long pair carries A (mother) and a (father): different alleles. The short pair carries B and B: the same allele.
INTERPHASE · S (DNA SYNTHESIS)Copy every chromosomeEach DNA molecule is used as a template to build an identical copy. The copy stays attached at the centromere.By the end of S: still 4 chromosomes, but 8 DNA molecules. In the cell, the DNA is unspooled the whole time; it is drawn as rods so you can follow it.
INTERPHASE · G2 (GAP 2)Get ready to divideEvery chromosome is now two sister chromatids carrying the same allele: A and A, a and a, B and B, B and B.The cell keeps growing, and the centrosome has been copied, ready to build the spindle.
M PHASE · PROPHASECondense, and build the spindleThe chromosomes condense into compact shapes you can see. The mitotic spindle grows from two poles.At the end of prophase the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibers attach at the centromeres (the textbook calls this part prometaphase).
M PHASE · METAPHASELine up in the middleEach replicated chromosome lines up separately, one above another, in the middle of the cell. Each is attached to fibers from both poles.Homologs do not pair up in mitosis. Still 4 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules.
M PHASE · ANAPHASESisters pulled apartThe centromeres split and the sister chromatids separate, pulled to opposite poles. Each chromatid is now its own chromosome.For a moment the cell holds 8 chromosomes: A, a, B, B on each side.
M PHASE · TELOPHASETwo new nucleiA nuclear envelope forms around each set, and the chromosomes start to unspool again. Each nucleus has A, a, B and B.The cell starts to pinch in at the middle.
M PHASE · CYTOKINESISTwo identical daughter cellsThe cytoplasm divides. Each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes, 4 DNA molecules, alleles A a B B: exactly what the parent had in G1.Each daughter starts again in G1, and the cycle repeats.
INTERPHASEG1 + S + G2Everything except M phase. The cell grows, copies its DNA and prepares.
M PHASEMitosis + cytokinesisProphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase divide the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cell.
WHAT TO WATCHCount as you go: chromosomes stay at 4 until anaphase, while DNA molecules go 4 → 8 in S and back to 4 per daughter cell. The alleles never change: A a B B in, A a B B out.
WHEN DO MUTATIONS HAPPEN?Mutations happen by chance, mostly as copying errors when DNA is replicated in S phase. They can also happen during mitosis. Module 3.2 covers them.
Check yourself: A cell is in G2. What did each chromosome look like in G1, and what will happen to it next?

In G1 each chromosome was one DNA molecule. S phase copied it, so in G2 it is two sister chromatids. Next comes M phase, where the sisters are pulled apart so each daughter cell gets one.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Interphase

The part of the cell cycle between one M phase and the next: G1, S and G2. The cell grows, copies its DNA and gets ready to divide.

S-phase

The phase of interphase in which DNA is synthesized: every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids.

M-phase

The part of the cell cycle in which the cell divides: mitosis followed by cytokinesis.

Cytokinesis

Division of the cytoplasm, which splits one cell into two daughter cells. It follows mitosis.

UNSPOOLED FOR READING, CONDENSED FOR MOVING

Chromosome condensation through the cell cycle

During interphase the cell is using its genes, so the DNA is spread out. Only when the cell is about to divide does each chromosome coil up into a compact shape you can see.

INTERACTIVE · ONE CHROMOSOME, THREE STATES

From thread to package

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
INTERPHASE · BEFORE SA long, open threadThe chromosome is one long DNA molecule, unspooled so the cell can read its genes. Chromosomes are not visible under a microscope now.
INTERPHASE · AFTER SCopied, still openAfter replication there are two identical DNA molecules: gene 1 and an exact copy of gene 1. They are still unspooled.
START OF MITOSISPacked up to moveThe two molecules condense into a compact replicated chromosome: two sister chromatids held together at the centromere. Packed this way, they can be moved without tangling.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Sister chromatids

The two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome. They are made in S phase and held together at the centromere until they separate in mitosis.

Centromere

The constriction that holds the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome together. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.

COUNT IT

Chromosomes vs. DNA molecules

Exam questions turn on one counting rule. A replicated chromosome is still one chromosome, but it is two DNA molecules.

INTERACTIVE · COUNT BEFORE AND AFTER

Count centromeres, then count chromatids

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
BEFORE S PHASE1 chromosome, 1 DNA moleculeAn unreplicated chromosome: one centromere, one DNA molecule.
AFTER S PHASEStill 1 chromosome, now 2 DNA moleculesReplication doubled the DNA but not the number of chromosomes: there is still one centromere, so it is one chromosome, made of two sister chromatids.
AFTER THE SISTERS SEPARATENow each chromatid is a chromosomeWhen mitosis pulls the sisters apart, each one has its own centromere and counts as a full chromosome.
THE RULEChromosomes = centromeres. DNA molecules = chromatids. A replicated chromosome has 2 sister chromatids, so 2 DNA molecules.
Try it on this cell in metaphase.
Check yourself: How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules does the cell above show?

3 chromosomes and 6 DNA molecules. Count the centromeres: 3. Each chromosome is two sister chromatids, so 3 × 2 = 6 DNA molecules.

Check yourself: An unreplicated linear chromosome goes through S phase. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules come out?

1 chromosome, 2 DNA molecules. It is now two sister chromatids held together at one centromere.

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. The cell cycle: G1 → S → G2 → M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, cytokinesis). Interphase = G1 + S + G2.
  2. G1: grow. S: replicate every chromosome. G2: get ready. M: mitosis, then cytokinesis.
  3. In interphase chromosomes are unspooled and not visible. They condense at the start of mitosis.
  4. S phase: one chromosome stays one chromosome but goes from 1 to 2 DNA molecules: two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
  5. Count centromeres for chromosomes, chromatids for DNA molecules.
  6. Mutations happen by chance, mostly as copying errors in S phase.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 3

Mitosis, haploid and diploid

THE QUESTION How does mitosis make sure each daughter cell gets exactly one copy of every chromosome, and how can you tell what kind of cell you are looking at?

In this part: the mitosis drawings to know, alleles that match or differ, haploid vs. diploid, how fertilization makes a diploid cell, the human karyotype, and where mitosis fits in a life cycle.

M PHASE

Mitosis: the drawings to know

Exam questions ask you to draw the same cell four times: before DNA replication, after it, at metaphase, and as the two daughter cells. Here is that set for the cell from the cell cycle step. Draw it yourself with two colors, one for each parent. To see every stage in between, tap through the complete cycle in Part 2.

DIAGRAM · FOUR DRAWINGS OF ONE CELL

Before S, after S, metaphase, daughters

PROPHASECondenseChromosomes condense and become visible; the spindle forms; the nuclear envelope breaks down.
METAPHASELine upEach replicated chromosome lines up separately in the middle, attached to both poles.
ANAPHASESeparateSister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
TELOPHASE + CYTOKINESISSplitTwo nuclei form, then the cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
WHAT TO TRACKJust three moments. After S: each chromosome is two sisters. Metaphase: they line up separately. Anaphase: the sisters separate, one copy to each side.
GO DEEPERThe textbook gives the end of prophase its own name, prometaphase: the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle attaches at the centromeres.
Check yourself: A cell with 5 replicated chromosomes in G2 goes through mitosis. How many chromosomes are in the nucleus of each daughter cell?

5. Each of the 5 is split into its two sister chromatids, and one of each goes to each daughter. Mitosis keeps the number the same.

Check yourself: Is the parent cell in these drawings haploid or diploid, and how can you tell from the metaphase drawing?

Diploid (2n = 4). At metaphase there are two long and two short chromosomes: two homologous pairs.

SISTERS VS. HOMOLOGS

Sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, genes and alleles

Most of your cells have two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Keep three ideas apart: sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, and alleles.

INTERACTIVE · TWO PAIRS AFTER S PHASE

Same allele or different?

Tap a button to explore
SISTER CHROMATIDSAlways the same alleleSister chromatids are copies made by replication in S phase, so they carry the same allele of every gene: A and A. That is true for every pair of sisters, unless a new mutation happened.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESA pair, one from each parentTwo chromosomes carrying the same set of genes: one inherited from your mother, one from your father. Their DNA is nearly identical, not identical, so their alleles can differ.
DIFFERENT ALLELES · A AND aSame gene, two versionsThe long pair carries the same gene at the same place, but the mother's version is A and the father's is a. Two different alleles of one gene.
THE SAME ALLELE · B AND BSame gene, same versionThe short pair carries B from the mother and B from the father. The homologs still came from two parents, but here they happen to carry the same allele.
TAP A LABELCopies always match; pairs may notA gene is a stretch of DNA carrying the information for one product. An allele is one version of that gene. Tap each label to see when two alleles are the same and when they differ.
COMMON MIX-UPSister chromatids are copies made in S phase. Homologous chromosomes are a pair you inherited from two parents. Homologs are not copies of each other.
Check yourself: If no mutations have occurred, do two sister chromatids carry the same allele or different alleles of each gene?

The same allele. They were copied from one DNA molecule.

Check yourself: Can you have two different alleles of the same gene in your cells?

Yes. You have one homologous chromosome from each parent, and the two can carry different alleles, such as A from your mother and a from your father.

Check yourself: After S phase but before M phase, how many copies of each gene does a diploid cell have, and how many alleles?

4 copies: two homologs, each made of two sister chromatids. But at most 2 alleles: the sisters carry the same allele, so A, A, a, a is two alleles.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.

Allele

One version of a gene. Different alleles have slightly different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of every gene, one on each homologous chromosome.

ONE SET OR TWO?

Haploid vs. diploid

A haploid cell (n) has one complete set of chromosomes. A diploid cell (2n) has two complete sets, so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. To tell them apart, look for pairs.

INTERACTIVE · SORT FIVE CELLS

Haploid or diploid?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
CELL 1 · HAPLOID, n = 3No pairsThree chromosomes, every one different. One set, so haploid.
CELL 2 · DIPLOID, 2n = 6Three pairsEach chromosome has a match of the same length and genes: three homologous pairs, two sets. Diploid.
CELL 3 · HAPLOID, n = 2Replicated, but still no pairsTwo replicated chromosomes that are different from each other. Being replicated does not make a cell diploid: the two sisters are copies, not a pair. Haploid.
CELL 4 · HAPLOID, n = 3Read the genesIn metaphase the chromosomes carry genes g, e and f. Each gene appears on only one chromosome (twice, on its two sisters), so there are no homologous pairs. Haploid.
CELL 5 · CAN'T TELLTwo chromosomes, no labelsFrom the number alone, you can't tell. If the two are homologs carrying the same genes, it is diploid (2n = 2). If they carry different genes, it is haploid (n = 2).
HOW TO TELLCount pairs, not chromosomes. Matching chromosomes with the same genes means diploid. All different means haploid.
Check yourself: Can a haploid cell go through mitosis? Can a diploid cell?

Yes, both. Mitosis copies whatever chromosomes a cell has and gives each daughter the same set. A haploid cell makes haploid daughters, and a diploid cell makes diploid daughters.

Check yourself: Are your somatic cells haploid or diploid?

Diploid. Your somatic cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Only your gametes, eggs or sperm, are haploid.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Haploid

A cell with one complete set of chromosomes (n). Every chromosome carries a different set of genes, so there are no homologous pairs.

Diploid

A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes (2n), so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Most human cells are diploid.

WHERE THE PAIRS COME FROM

Egg meets sperm: fertilization makes a diploid cell

Why do your chromosomes come in pairs, one from each parent? Because you started as two haploid cells that fused.

INTERACTIVE · FROM TWO HAPLOID CELLS TO ONE DIPLOID CELL

n + n = 2n

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
TWO GAMETES · BOTH HAPLOIDOne set eachThe mother's egg carries one set of chromosomes (n = 2): a long one with allele A and a short one with B. The father's sperm also carries one set: a long one with a and a short one with B.
FERTILIZATIONThe two cells fuseAt fertilization the sperm and egg fuse. Their chromosomes end up in one cell: n + n = 2n.
THE ZYGOTE · DIPLOIDNow every chromosome has a partnerThe fertilized egg, the zygote, is diploid (2n = 4). Each long chromosome has a long partner and each short one a short partner: two homologous pairs, one member from each parent.Mitosis then copies this exact set into every cell of the body.
ALLELES · SAME OR DIFFERENTIt depends on the parentsThe long pair got A from the egg and a from the sperm: different alleles. The short pair got B from both: the same allele.So a diploid cell always has two alleles of every gene, and they may match or differ.
EGGHaploid (n)One set of chromosomes, from the mother.
SPERMHaploid (n)One set of chromosomes, from the father.
ZYGOTEDiploid (2n)Two sets: homologous pairs, one from each parent.
WHERE THE GAMETES COME FROMEggs and sperm are made by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. That is Module 3.2.
Check yourself: An egg carries alleles A and B; a sperm carries a and B. What alleles does the zygote have?

A, a, B and B. One of each pair from each parent: different alleles for the first gene, the same allele for the second.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Gametes

Haploid reproductive cells: eggs and sperm. They are made by meiosis, and two of them fuse at fertilization.

Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilization, so the offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

THE HUMAN SET

Reading a karyotype

A karyotype is a picture of all of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs. It is made during mitosis, when the chromosomes are condensed and visible.

INTERACTIVE · A HUMAN KARYOTYPE (SKETCH)

46 chromosomes in 23 pairs

Tap a button to explore
COUNT46 chromosomesHuman somatic cells have 46 chromosomes: 22 numbered pairs, sorted from longest (1) to shortest (22), plus one pair of sex chromosomes.
ONE PAIRChromosome 1, twiceThere are two copies of chromosome 1, two of chromosome 2, and so on. Each pair is a homologous pair: one from the mother, one from the father. So human somatic cells are diploid.
SEX CHROMOSOMESX and YThe sex chromosomes are X and Y: XX in genetic females, XY in genetic males. X and Y form a pair but carry different sets of genes, the one exception to homologs having the same genes.

Check yourself: How many total alleles per gene does a diploid cell have in G1?

2. One on each chromosome of the homologous pair. (They may be the same allele or two different ones.)

THE BIG PICTURE

Mitosis in a life cycle

Where does mitosis fit in a whole life? In humans it builds and maintains the body. Making gametes takes a different division, meiosis, which is the next module.

INTERACTIVE · THE HUMAN LIFE CYCLE

Two kinds of division, one cycle

Tap a button to explore
MITOSISBuilds the whole bodyA new person starts as one cell, the diploid zygote. It divides by mitosis again and again into every cell of the body, all diploid with the same chromosomes.That includes most cells, the somatic cells (skin, gut, blood), and a few germ cells set aside in the ovaries or testes. So yes, mitosis comes first: the germ cells themselves were made by mitosis.
MEIOSISOnly the germ cells, years laterSomatic cells never do meiosis. Only the germ cells do, turning diploid cells into haploid gametes, eggs or sperm, each with one set of chromosomes. Module 3.2 shows how.
FERTILIZATIONBack to diploid, the next generationIn sexual reproduction, a haploid egg from one parent and a haploid sperm from the other fuse. The new zygote is diploid again, one set from each parent, and the cycle starts over for a new person.
TAP A STEPWhere each division happensMitosis keeps the chromosome number. Meiosis halves it. Fertilization doubles it back. Tap each one.
SCENE · DIFFERENT CELLS, SAME DNA

Does a skin cell have different DNA from a liver cell?

No. Every somatic cell came from the same zygote by mitosis, so they all have the same DNA, except for any new mutations. Cells differ in which genes they use, not in which genes they have.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Somatic cells

The cells of the body other than the cells that make gametes. Human somatic cells are diploid and are made by mitosis.

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Mitosis: prophase (condense, spindle forms), metaphase (line up separately in the middle), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase (two nuclei), then cytokinesis.
  2. Each daughter cell gets one copy of every chromosome: the same DNA and alleles as the parent.
  3. Sister chromatids are identical copies (same allele). Homologous chromosomes are a pair from mother and father (same genes, alleles can differ).
  4. A gene is a stretch of DNA for one product. An allele is one version of it. A diploid cell has 2 alleles of every gene.
  5. Haploid (n): one set, no pairs. Diploid (2n): homologous pairs. Both can go through mitosis. Look for pairs to tell them apart.
  6. Fertilization: a haploid egg (n) + a haploid sperm (n) = a diploid zygote (2n). Each pair gets one chromosome from each parent, so its two alleles can be the same (B and B) or different (A and a).
  7. Humans: 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs (22 numbered + XX or XY). Somatic cells are diploid; gametes are haploid.
  8. Every somatic cell has the same DNA; cells differ in which genes they use.
Vocab · 24 terms
Unicellular Made of a single cell. For a unicellular organism, cell division is reproduction.
Multicellular Made of many cells, like animals, plants and most fungi. Only eukaryotes are multicellular. Cell division builds and repairs the body; reproduction is a separate job.
Mitosis Division of the nucleus in which the sister chromatids of every chromosome are pulled apart, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent cell.
Meiosis The cell division that turns a diploid cell into four haploid gametes, whose DNA is different from the parent cell's.
Plasmid A small circle of DNA in a prokaryotic cell, separate from the chromosome. It usually carries genes that are not essential for the species.
Chromosome One double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins. It carries many genes. After S phase it is two sister chromatids, but it still counts as one chromosome.
Nuclear DNA The DNA in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, organized into linear chromosomes. In eukaryotes, "genome" usually means the nuclear DNA.
Conjugation A way prokaryotes share DNA: one cell passes a copy of some of its DNA, often a plasmid, to another cell through a connecting bridge. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction.
Asexual reproduction Reproduction by one parent alone, by mitosis (or binary fission in prokaryotes). The offspring have the same DNA as the parent, except new mutations.
Genotype The alleles an organism carries for a gene or genes, written as letters such as Hh. Clones have the same genotype.
Phenotype What an organism looks like or does: its observable traits, such as hair shape. It depends on the genotype and on the environment.
Interphase The part of the cell cycle between one M phase and the next: G1, S and G2. The cell grows, copies its DNA and gets ready to divide.
S-phase The phase of interphase in which DNA is synthesized: every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids.
M-phase The part of the cell cycle in which the cell divides: mitosis followed by cytokinesis.
Cytokinesis Division of the cytoplasm, which splits one cell into two daughter cells. It follows mitosis.
Sister chromatids The two identical DNA molecules of a replicated chromosome. They are made in S phase and held together at the centromere until they separate in mitosis.
Centromere The constriction that holds the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome together. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.
Homologous chromosome One of a pair of chromosomes that carry the same set of genes, one inherited from the mother and one from the father. Their DNA is nearly identical, so their alleles can differ.
Allele One version of a gene. Different alleles have slightly different DNA sequences. A diploid cell has two alleles of every gene, one on each homologous chromosome.
Haploid A cell with one complete set of chromosomes (n). Every chromosome carries a different set of genes, so there are no homologous pairs.
Diploid A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes (2n), so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. Most human cells are diploid.
Gametes Haploid reproductive cells: eggs and sperm. They are made by meiosis, and two of them fuse at fertilization.
Somatic cells The cells of the body other than the cells that make gametes. Human somatic cells are diploid and are made by mitosis.
Sexual reproduction Reproduction in which two haploid gametes fuse at fertilization, so the offspring gets one set of chromosomes from each parent.

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · The eukaryotic cell cycle2 · Haploid and diploid3 · Mitosis, drawn out4 · Genes and alleles5 · What mitosis and binary fission are for6 · Reading a karyotype7 · Large numbers of chromosomes8 · Cell division in a life cycle9 · How genetic material is arranged10 · Who divides how, and two ways to reproduce11 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Every cell division copies the DNA, then shares it out. Bacteria do it by binary fission. Eukaryotes copy every chromosome in S phase and split the sister chromatids in mitosis, so each daughter cell gets the same DNA as the parent. Diploid cells carry chromosomes in homologous pairs, one from each parent.

SECTION 1OBJECTIVES 1 AND 2

The eukaryotic cell cycle

  • G1 (gap 1): the cell grows and replicates its organelles. Each chromosome is one DNA molecule.
  • S (DNA synthesis): every chromosome is replicated into two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
  • G2 (gap 2): the cell keeps growing and prepares to divide. Each chromosome is two sister chromatids.
  • M: mitosis (the nucleus divides), then cytokinesis (the cytoplasm divides). Each daughter starts again in G1.
  • Interphase = G1 + S + G2. Checkpoints make sure the cell is ready before it moves on.
  • In interphase, chromosomes are unspooled so genes can be read, and they are not visible under a microscope. They condense at the start of mitosis.
PHASEEACH CHROMOSOME ISDNA MOLECULES PER CHROMOSOME
G1Unreplicated1
SBeing copied1 → 2
G2Replicated: 2 sister chromatids2
M, after anaphaseSeparated: each chromatid is now a chromosome1
COUNTING RULEChromosomes = centromeres. DNA molecules = chromatids. Replication doubles the DNA, not the number of chromosomes.
  • Mutations happen by chance, mostly as copying errors when DNA is replicated in S phase; they can also happen during mitosis.
SECTION 2OBJECTIVE 3

Haploid and diploid

  • Haploid (n): one complete set of chromosomes. Every chromosome carries a different set of genes; there are no pairs.
  • Diploid (2n): two complete sets, so chromosomes come in homologous pairs, one from each parent.
  • How to tell: look for pairs of matching chromosomes (same size, same genes). Replicated sister chromatids are copies, not a pair.
  • A cell with only 2 chromosomes: you can't tell from the number alone. Homologous → diploid (2n = 2). Different genes → haploid (n = 2).
  • Both haploid and diploid cells can go through mitosis. Your somatic cells are diploid; gametes are haploid.
SECTION 3OBJECTIVE 4

Mitosis, drawn out

  • Start (G1): each chromosome unreplicated. After S: each chromosome is two sister chromatids with the same allele.
  • Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible; the mitotic spindle forms from two poles; the nuclear envelope breaks down (the textbook calls that part prometaphase).
  • Metaphase: each replicated chromosome lines up separately in the middle, attached to spindle fibers from both poles.
  • Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles. Each is now a chromosome.
  • Telophase: a nuclear envelope forms around each set. Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm splits into two daughter cells.
  • Result: two daughter cells with the same chromosomes and alleles as the parent cell.
STAGECELL WITH 2n = 2CHROMOSOMESDNA MOLECULES
G1A and a, unreplicated22
After SA A and a a24
Metaphaselined up separately24
Anaphasesisters pulled apart44
Each daughterA and a22
SISTER CHROMATIDSTwo identical copies made in S phase. Same allele. Held together at the centromere until anaphase.
HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMESA pair, one from the mother and one from the father. Same genes, nearly identical DNA, so alleles can differ.
SECTION 4OBJECTIVE 5

Genes and alleles

  • A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying the information for one product. Each chromosome carries many genes.
  • An allele is one version of a gene. Alleles of the same gene have slightly different DNA sequences.
  • Each chromosome has one allele per gene. A diploid cell has 2 alleles of every gene, one on each homolog. They can be the same or different.
  • After S phase, a diploid cell has 4 copies of each gene but still at most 2 alleles, because sister chromatids carry the same allele.
  • Exception: the X and Y sex chromosomes form a pair but carry different sets of genes.
DIFFERENT ALLELESThe long pair in the example cell: A from the mother, a from the father. Same gene, different versions.
THE SAME ALLELEThe short pair: B from the mother and B from the father. Homologs can match. Sister chromatids always match, because one was copied from the other.
SECTION 5OBJECTIVE 6

What mitosis and binary fission are for

  • Why cells divide: reproduction (one-celled organisms, and asexual reproduction in some species), development and growth from a single fertilized egg, and repair and regeneration of tissues.
  • Every division has two parts: replication of the DNA, then segregation of the copies into two daughter cells.
  • Binary fission (bacteria, archaea, and mitochondria and chloroplasts): the circular DNA is attached to the membrane; it is copied, the cell grows so the copies move apart, and the cell pinches in two. It is regulated by nutrient availability.
  • Mitosis (eukaryotes): needed because the DNA is in a nucleus on several linear chromosomes, so the copies must be pulled apart by the spindle.
MITOSISMEIOSIS
Divisions12 in a row: meiosis I (homologous pairs split), meiosis II (sister chromatids split)
Daughter cells24 (gametes)
DNA vs. the parentIdentical (except new mutations)Different
Chromosome numberKept: 2n → 2nHalved: 2n → n
WhereSomatic cellsOnly germ cells
What forGrowth, repair, asexual reproductionSexual reproduction
SECTION 6OBJECTIVE 7

Reading a karyotype

  • A karyotype is a picture of all of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs. It is made during mitosis, when they are condensed and visible.
  • Human somatic cells: 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 numbered pairs, longest (1) to shortest (22), plus the sex chromosomes, XX or XY.
  • Two copies of each numbered chromosome means human somatic cells are diploid.
  • Before S phase each chromosome (1) has many genes, (2) has one allele per gene, (3) is a single double-stranded DNA molecule.
SECTION 7OBJECTIVE 8

Large numbers of chromosomes

  • The logic doesn't change with the number. A horse cell has 64 chromosomes: 64 DNA molecules in G1, 128 after S, and each daughter cell gets 64 after mitosis.
  • A human cell: 46 chromosomes in G1 (46 DNA molecules), 46 chromosomes but 92 DNA molecules in G2, 46 in each daughter.
  • Mitosis never changes the chromosome number: a cell with 5 replicated chromosomes in G2 gives daughters with 5 each.
SECTION 8OBJECTIVE 9

Cell division in a life cycle

  • Humans: a diploid zygote (fertilized egg) divides by mitosis many times to build every somatic cell.
  • Meiosis in germ cells makes haploid gametes (eggs and sperm). At fertilization two gametes fuse into a new diploid zygote: sexual reproduction.
  • Every somatic cell came from the same zygote, so skin, muscle, heart and liver cells all have the same DNA, except new mutations. They differ in which genes they use.
CELLPLOIDYCHROMOSOMES IN THE EXAMPLE
EggHaploid, n = 2long A, short B
SpermHaploid, n = 2long a, short B
Zygote (egg + sperm)Diploid, 2n = 4long pair A and a, short pair B and B
n + n = 2nFertilization is what makes a cell diploid: each homologous pair is one chromosome from the egg and one from the sperm.
SECTION 9OBJECTIVE 10

How genetic material is arranged

PROKARYOTESEUKARYOTES
DomainsBacteria, ArchaeaEukarya (unicellular or multicellular)
NucleusNoneYes, plus other compartments
ChromosomesOne circular chromosomeUsually more than one linear chromosome
Extra DNAPlasmids: small, usually non-essential genesCircular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts
How they divideBinary fissionMitosis (somatic cells); meiosis (germ cells only)
  • Each chromosome is one double-stranded DNA molecule packaged with proteins, carrying many genes.
  • In eukaryotes, genome usually means the nuclear DNA.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA because they descend from engulfed bacteria; they still divide by binary fission.
  • Where vs. form vs. stage: prokaryote DNA is in one place (the cytoplasm); eukaryote DNA is in the nucleus (linear) and in mitochondria and chloroplasts (circular). Nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene are zoom levels, not places. The cell cycle changes the packing (loose threads in interphase, condensed in mitosis), not the place.
SECTION 10

Who divides how, and two ways to reproduce

  • Three domains: Bacteria and Archaea (prokaryotes, always unicellular) and Eukarya (eukaryotes, unicellular like yeast and amoebas, or multicellular like animals, plants and most fungi). Archaea are the closest relatives of eukaryotes.
  • Prokaryotes: binary fission only, never mitosis or meiosis.
  • Eukaryotes that reproduce sexually: mitosis in somatic cells and meiosis in germ cells, both in the same organism. Reproduction = meiosis + fertilization.
  • Eukaryotes that reproduce asexually: mitosis only, no meiosis (yeast budding, strawberry runners, aphids). Many species do both.
  • Asexual reproduction: one parent, no mate; offspring are clones (same genotype). Sexual reproduction: two parents; meiosis deals each gamete one allele of every gene, so every child is a new combination.
  • Genotype = the alleles an organism carries (PP, Pp). Phenotype = what it looks like. PP and Pp can look the same; clones can look different in different environments. Phenotype = genotype + environment.
  • Genetically identical copies: binary fission and mitosis. Recombination: conjugation in prokaryotes (DNA passed between cells, not reproduction) and meiosis + fertilization in eukaryotes.
ASEXUALSEXUAL
ParentsOneTwo
DivisionBinary fission or mitosisMeiosis, then fertilization
OffspringClonesEvery genotype different
AdvantagesSaves energy, no mates, faster growthGenetic variability, rapid adaptation
DisadvantagesLow variability, slow to adaptCosts energy, only females have young
SECTION 11

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Draw the cell cycle with G1, S, G2 and M, mark interphase, and say what each chromosome looks like in each phase.
  • Given a cell at one stage, say what its chromosomes looked like before and will look like after.
  • Tell a haploid cell from a diploid cell in a drawing, including a replicated cell and a cell with only two chromosomes.
  • Draw mitosis for a cell with two chromosomes, before and after S, at metaphase and in the daughter cells, and point out sister chromatids and homologs.
  • Explain the difference between a gene and an allele, and count alleles and gene copies before and after S.
  • Give at least three reasons cells divide, and describe binary fission and what regulates its speed.
  • Compare mitosis and meiosis: number of cells, DNA, ploidy, where and why.
  • Read a human karyotype: count, pairs and sex chromosomes.
  • Count chromosomes and DNA molecules for any number of chromosomes (64, 46, 20) through the cycle.
  • Place mitosis, meiosis and fertilization in a human life cycle.
  • Show how a haploid egg and a haploid sperm make a diploid zygote, and point out which pairs carry the same allele and which carry different alleles.
  • Compare how DNA is organized in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and explain why mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA.
  • Name the three domains, give unicellular and multicellular examples, and say which kind of division each group uses.
  • Say what meiosis I and meiosis II each separate, and why they are not generations.
  • Compare asexual and sexual reproduction, and tell genotype from phenotype.
COMMON MIX-UPMitosis gives 2 identical daughter cells. Meiosis gives 4 different gametes. And sister chromatids are copies, while homologous chromosomes are a pair from two parents.

Infographics

Every diagram from the flow charts in one place, without the reading in between. Start with the one-page map, then scan the rest.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
MODULE 3.1 · PART 1

Why and how cells divide

Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. How does one cell become two, each with a complete copy of the DNA, and which cells divide which way?

1Why do cells divide?
Every cell comes from a cell that already existed. Cell division is how one cell becomes two, and there are several reasons a living thing needs it.
2Replication, then segregation
Whatever the reason, and whatever kind of cell, every cell division has the same two parts. First the cell copies its DNA. Then it hands one copy to each daughter cell.
4Binary fission, mitosis and meiosis
There are three kinds of cell division. Which one a cell uses depends on whether it is a prokaryote or a eukaryote, and, in eukaryotes, on whether it is a body cell or a germ cell.
6Genetically identical copies vs. recombination
Every way of handling DNA either makes genetically identical copies (same DNA out) or causes recombination (new combinations of genes). Prokaryotes and eukaryotes each have a way to do both, but only eukaryotes recombine while making offspring.
5Asexual vs. sexual reproduction
"Asexual" and "sexual" describe how a whole organism makes offspring, not a kind of cell. A strawberry plant sending out runners is reproducing asexually, by mitosis. Two people having a child are reproducing sexually, by meiosis and fertilization.
3Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
Every living thing belongs to one of three domains. Two of them, bacteria and archaea, are prokaryotes; the third is the eukaryotes. Which group an organism is in tells you where its DNA is and how its cells divide.
7Binary fission, step by step
Bacteria and archaea divide by binary fission. It has the same two jobs, replication and segregation, and it is the simplest way to do them.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 2

The eukaryotic cell cycle

Before a eukaryotic cell can divide, every chromosome has to be copied. When does that happen, and what does a chromosome look like before and after?

1The cell cycle, G1 to cytokinesis
A eukaryotic cell does not divide whenever it likes. Its life runs in a cycle, and checkpoints make sure it is ready before each stage. Follow one cell all the way round: it has 4 chromosomes, a long pair and a short pair, one of each pair from the mother (pink) and one from the father (blue).
2Chromosome condensation through the cell cycle
During interphase the cell is using its genes, so the DNA is spread out. Only when the cell is about to divide does each chromosome coil up into a compact shape you can see.
3Chromosomes vs. DNA molecules
Exam questions turn on one counting rule. A replicated chromosome is still one chromosome, but it is two DNA molecules.
MODULE 3.1 · PART 3

Mitosis, haploid and diploid

How does mitosis make sure each daughter cell gets exactly one copy of every chromosome, and how can you tell what kind of cell you are looking at?

1Mitosis: the drawings to know
Exam questions ask you to draw the same cell four times: before DNA replication, after it, at metaphase, and as the two daughter cells. Here is that set for the cell from the cell cycle step. Draw it yourself with two colors, one for each parent. To see every stage in between, tap through the complete cycle in Part 2.
2Sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, genes and alleles
Most of your cells have two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Keep three ideas apart: sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, and alleles.
3Haploid vs. diploid
A haploid cell (n) has one complete set of chromosomes. A diploid cell (2n) has two complete sets, so its chromosomes come in homologous pairs. To tell them apart, look for pairs.
4Egg meets sperm: fertilization makes a diploid cell
Why do your chromosomes come in pairs, one from each parent? Because you started as two haploid cells that fused.
5Reading a karyotype
A karyotype is a picture of all of a cell's chromosomes, sorted into pairs. It is made during mitosis, when the chromosomes are condensed and visible.
6Mitosis in a life cycle
Where does mitosis fit in a whole life? In humans it builds and maintains the body. Making gametes takes a different division, meiosis, which is the next module.

Copy, then share

Binary fission, mitosis and meiosis
INFOGRAPHIC 4
THREE KINDS OF ORGANISM

Who divides how?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEABinary fission, and that's itA bacterium or an archaeon is unicellular: one cell is the whole organism. To reproduce, it copies its DNA and splits in two by binary fission. That is asexual reproduction: one parent, two identical offspring.Prokaryotes have no nucleus and never do mitosis or meiosis.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE SEXUALLYMitosis and meiosis in the same bodyIn an animal or a flowering plant, the somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis: 2 identical cells, for growth and repair. Only the germ cells (in ovaries and testes, or in flowers) divide by meiosis: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes, all different.Here mitosis is not reproduction. Reproduction is meiosis (to make gametes) plus fertilization, a gamete from each of two parents.
EUKARYOTES THAT REPRODUCE ASEXUALLYMitosis only, no meiosisMany eukaryotes also make offspring by mitosis alone: yeast grows buds, a strawberry plant sends out runners, and female aphids have young without mating. One parent, no mate, and the offspring are clones.Many species do both, depending on conditions (strawberries also flower). So prokaryotes are always asexual, but eukaryotes can be asexual, sexual or both.
INFOGRAPHIC 5
INTERACTIVE · SIDE BY SIDE

Three kinds of division

Tap a button to explore
BINARY FISSION · PROKARYOTESBacteria and archaeaWho: prokaryotes, which are bacteria and archaea (for cell division they work the same way). Also mitochondria and chloroplasts inside eukaryotic cells.The DNA: one circular chromosome (plus plasmids), no nucleus, attached to the cell membrane.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent. For a one-celled prokaryote, that is reproduction.
MITOSIS · EUKARYOTESSomatic (body) cellsWho: eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists), in their somatic (body) cells. In a eukaryote that reproduces asexually, mitosis is also how it makes offspring.The DNA: several linear chromosomes inside a nucleus.Result: 2 cells with the same DNA as the parent (2n → 2n), for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
MEIOSIS · EUKARYOTESGerm cells onlyWho: eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, and only in germ cells, the cells that make eggs and sperm. The same organism does mitosis in all its other cells: that is why the dashed box joins the two.Two divisions in a row: meiosis I splits each homologous pair (A from a) into 2 cells; meiosis II splits the sister chromatids, like mitosis, into 4 gametes. No DNA copying in between.The DNA: linear chromosomes in a nucleus, in homologous pairs (A from the mother, a from the father).Result: 4 gametes, each with half the chromosomes (2n → n) and different DNA, for sexual reproduction. How it works is Module 3.2.
ALL THREETwo categories, same two jobsBinary fission is its own category (prokaryotes). Mitosis and meiosis belong together (eukaryotes). Each one replicates the DNA and then segregates the copies. Binary fission segregates by the cell growing; mitosis and meiosis need a spindle to pull chromosomes apart.
TAP ONEWhich cells do which?Prokaryotes do only binary fission. Eukaryotes do mitosis and meiosis, never binary fission (except inside their mitochondria and chloroplasts).
Genetically identical copies vs. recombination
INFOGRAPHIC 6
INTERACTIVE · TWO JOBS × TWO KINDS OF CELL

Identical copies or recombination?

Tap a button to explore
PROKARYOTES · BACTERIA AND ARCHAEACopy by dividing, recombine without dividingCopy: binary fission makes 2 cells with the same DNA. That is how prokaryotes reproduce.Recombine: separately, one cell can pass a copy of some DNA, often a plasmid, to another through a bridge: conjugation. No new cell is made, so it is not reproduction, and it is not meiosis.
EUKARYOTESMitosis copies, meiosis recombinesCopy: mitosis makes 2 cells with the same DNA, in body cells and in asexual reproduction.Recombine: meiosis deals each gamete a different combination of the parents' chromosomes, and fertilization joins two of them: sexual reproduction.
GENETICALLY IDENTICAL COPIESBinary fission and mitosis are the same ideaBoth copy the DNA and split it evenly: 2 identical cells. Binary fission is the prokaryote version, mitosis the eukaryote version. They differ in how the copies are pulled apart (membrane growth vs. a spindle).
RECOMBINATIONConjugation and meiosis both recombine genes, very differentlyConjugation (prokaryotes): DNA passes from one cell to another; no division, no gametes.Meiosis + fertilization (eukaryotes): chromosomes are shuffled into gametes, then two gametes fuse.
TAP A ROW OR COLUMNTwo ways to handle DNAIdentical copies keep the DNA the same. Recombination makes new combinations of genes. And mutation adds brand-new changes in all four.
Asexual vs. sexual reproduction
INFOGRAPHIC 7
ONE PARENT OR TWO · WHAT COMES OUT

Clones vs. a family

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
ASEXUAL REPRODUCTIONOne parent, identical offspringOne plant makes new plants by mitosis only, for example along runners. No second organism is needed. The offspring are clones: the same genotype as the parent, so they look the same too.The only way a clone differs is a new mutation, a chance change when the DNA is copied.
SEXUAL REPRODUCTIONTwo parents, a new mix every timeA female (♀) and a male (♂) each make gametes by meiosis, which deals each gamete one allele of every gene, at random. Fertilization joins an egg and a sperm.Here the mother is Hh Cc and the father hh cc, so four different kids are possible. Every child is a recombination of the parents' genes, not a copy of either one. (The hair genes are made up for the picture.)
GENOTYPE VS. PHENOTYPEThe letters vs. the lookEvery organism, plant, animal or microbe, has both. Genotype = the alleles it carries (PP, Pp, pp). Phenotype = what you can see or measure (purple flowers, height, spiky hair).Different genotypes can give the same phenotype: PP and Pp flowers are both purple, because P hides p (dominant and recessive alleles are Module 3.3). And the same genotype can give different phenotypes: two Pp clones grow tall in sun and short in shade.
INFOGRAPHIC 8
WHY TWO WAYS?

Fast copies vs. a shuffled deck

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
THE PRICE OF SEXAsexual populations grow fasterSay every female has 2 offspring. 100 asexual females make 200 offspring, all able to reproduce: the population doubles. 100 sexual individuals are about half males, so they make 100 offspring: the population only replaces itself.The cost comes from needing males (only females produce offspring), not from meiosis being a slower division.
THE SHUFFLEEvery gamete is a different handMeiosis deals each gamete one chromosome from every pair, at random. With 3 pairs there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 possible hands; with your 23 pairs, 2²³, about 8 million. Then fertilization combines two hands.
THE PAYOFFA moving targetParasites and viruses adapt to the host genotypes that are common. If every host is a copy, one virus that fits one fits all. If every host is a new shuffle, it fits only a few, and the next generation is shuffled again. That is why sex allows rapid adaptation to new environments and parasites.
Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes

Three domains, and what each one does

Tap a button to explore
BACTERIA · PROKARYOTESOne cell, no nucleusBacteria such as E. coli are always unicellular. Their DNA is one circular chromosome, often with plasmids, with no nucleus around it.They reproduce by binary fission, which is asexual, and can pass DNA to each other by conjugation.
ARCHAEA · PROKARYOTESLook like bacteria, related to usArchaea (for example the microbes that make methane in swamps and cow stomachs) are also unicellular prokaryotes with circular DNA, and also divide by binary fission.On the tree, though, archaea are the closest relatives of eukaryotes.
